summary: On Friday, August 14, 2026, Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty in Manhattan federal court to two stalking counts in the December 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, admitting to the shooting during the hearing.
Mangione researched the investor conference online, posed as an investor to obtain details, and used a 3D-printed pistol to ambush Thompson outside a Midtown hotel on December 4, 2024.

U.S. District Judge Margaret Garnett scheduled federal sentencing for December 18, 2026, while defense attorney Karen Friedman Agnifilo confirmed there was 'no deal' regarding the plea, leaving final penalty discretion to the court.

Following the plea, defense lawyers filed a motion to dismiss separate state murder charges citing New York's double jeopardy protections, though Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg's office plans to oppose the move.

The state murder trial remains scheduled for September 8, 2026, though the federal guilty plea creates significant uncertainty regarding its progression, as both cases could result in life imprisonment for Mangione.
title: Source Icon

summary: On Friday, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro announced that authorities arrested Melissa L. Farris for vandalizing the National World War II Memorial, which honors more than 400,000 Americans killed in World War II.
The vandalism occurred Thursday at the National Mall, where graffiti reading "Clean hands, dirty money" was spray-painted on the monument and soap clogged a fountain, forcing the memorial to close.

Pirro's office filed two felony charges against Farris: Depredation Against Property of the United States and Destruction of Veterans' Memorials, offenses carrying penalties of up to 10 years in prison.
The U.S. Department of the Interior called the act "an utter disgrace," while the Veterans of Foreign Wars described it as "a slap in the face" to veterans and their families.

President Donald Trump condemned the vandalism on Truth Social as a "grave insult," referencing his ongoing criticism of Pirro over her office's decision to drop charges in a separate Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool case.
title: Woman arrested and facing felony charges in World War II memorial vandalism case, DOJ says

summary: On Friday, President Donald Trump filed an emergency request with the Supreme Court to resume his $400 million White House ballroom project after lower courts halted above-ground construction.

Last week, the Circuit Court ordered Trump to stop above-ground work, ruling the project requires Congressional approval and constitutes unauthorized 'Executive self-help' without legislative authority.
Architect Shalom Baranes designed the ballroom at approximately 89,000 square feet, nearly double the Executive Mansion's 55,000 square feet. Trump aims to complete it by summer 2028.

Solicitor General John Sauer argued the construction is 'absolutely required' for presidential safety, calling the injunction 'judicial overreach.' The court paused its ruling for 14 days to allow the appeal.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation brought the case last year, arguing Congress never authorized the Executive Branch to reshape the White House. This marks the first Supreme Court challenge to Trump's projects.
title: Trump asks US Supreme Court to allow White House ballroom construction to continue

summary: On Thursday, the Kennedy Center board voted to inscribe "Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump" beneath the venue's signage while approving a two-year, $250 million renovation closure.

Executive Director Matt Floca recommended the two-year closure to address severe structural decay, including corrosion as thin as tissue paper. The $250 million project covers repairs, new marble floors, and $7 million in restroom upgrades.

District Judge Christopher Cooper will review these moves after previously blocking a closure he deemed "ill-informed and seemingly preordained." Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty denounced the plan as circumventing court rulings.
The inscription serves as a workaround to federal law banning new memorials at the site. Trump's name was removed in June after a court order, though tarps still cover the facade.
Kennedy Center officials must submit the renovation plan to Judge Cooper next week. These moves align with Trump's broader capital remodeling, including work at the East Wing and East Potomac Park.
title: Kennedy Center board reapproves Trump’s plan to close for renovations

summary: On Saturday, August 15, 2026, multiple suspects opened fire near the Quad Annexes at Virginia State University, wounding five people. One victim remains in critical condition while four others sustained non-life-threatening injuries.

Following the shooting, Chesterfield County Police are leading the investigation with assistance from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Hanover County Sheriff's Office. The campus lockdown was lifted at 8:20 a.m. Saturday.

Officials confirmed one victim is a VSU student, who has since been released from the hospital. The remaining four victims sustained non-life-threatening injuries and were transported to area hospitals shortly after the 1:30 a.m. incident.

Classes for the fall 2026 semester remain scheduled to begin on Monday, August 17, with residence halls already open for students. University officials hosted the 'New Trojans Experience' for incoming students on Friday, featuring NFL MVP Cam Newton as guest speaker.

Former director of distance education Arthur Fridrich said, 'To start a new year with this event is very tragic. It casts a shadow in the minds of all students.' The incident occurs as the historically Black university prepares for its academic year.
title: 5 people injured in shooting with multiple shooters at Virginia State University

summary: In a Friday filing in Carson City, The Gaming Control Board accused Kalshi of missing the August 12 deadline to block Nevada users, requesting the court impose fines of $120,000 a day for noncompliance.

Previously, Kalshi agreed to implement 'a robust, multi-source geofencing solution provided by a third-party commercial provider' to block Nevada residents, utilizing GeoComply, a Nevada-licensed technology company, to enforce restrictions.
Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford argued in his Friday motion that Kalshi's August 9 app update left insufficient time for compliance, since updates can take up to seven days to reach all users.

Kalshi General Counsel Rick Heaslip called the lawsuit 'a vindictive waste of taxpayer dollars,' alleging state investigators 'actively worked to circumvent' the company's blocking measures and violated federal law by misrepresenting their residence.
Pending a ruling by the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, Kalshi and two other prediction markets face uncertainty regarding the regulatory agency's ongoing effort to ban their Nevada operations.
title: Prediction market operator Kalshi hits back at Nevada regulator over geofencing fine

summary: On Saturday, Chesterfield County Police arrested 19-year-old Camron Harris after finding him hiding in a Virginia State University dormitory closet following an overnight shooting that wounded five people near the Quad Annexes.

Authorities obtained eight felony warrants for Harris, including malicious wounding and use of a firearm in the commission of a felony, with The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives assisting the investigation.
Police confirmed Harris and four of the five wounded individuals were not students; the university has about 5,700 students and sits 24 miles south of Richmond in Ettrick, Virginia.

Many students had just completed the "New Trojans Experience" orientation when the shooting occurred, prompting the university to state, "We recognize the concern this incident has caused among our students, parents, alumni, friends, and the broader VSU community."
Arthur Fridrich, the university's former director of distance education, called the event "very tragic," noting it "casts a shadow in the minds of all students" as classes resume on Monday.
title: Police say 19-year-old arrested in connection with Virginia State University shooting

summary: Investors are modeling an IPO valuation above $2 trillion for Anthropic , with some scenarios stretching as high as $3 trillion for the five-year-old maker of Claude.
The valuation hinges on projected 2028 revenue of roughly $190 billion to $200 billion, a figure that far exceeds the $47 billion revenue run rate Anthropic publicized in May.
Anthropic is reportedly in early talks to acquire Israeli startup Decart for $6 billion, a price 50% higher than the company's May valuation of nearly $4 billion.

Decart's software helps chips run more efficiently, which could reduce Anthropic's infrastructure costs and lower the expense of serving individual Claude requests without purchasing additional hardware.

David Merkel, a principal at investment firm Aleph Investments, questioned whether AI productivity justifies such valuations, noting the market is entertaining prices once reserved for industrial empires.
title: Anthropic IPO valuation hinges on $190-200 billion 2028 revenue forecast: Reuters

summary: On Friday, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to reverse lower court rulings halting construction of the East Wing ballroom, arguing the $600 million project is critical for hosting world leaders securely.

A federal court ruled last week that the National Trust for Historic Preservation suit must halt construction due to lack of congressional approval; the project began last year after Trump ordered the East Wing demolished.

Trump attacked the National Trust on Truth Social, calling the group "TREASONISTS" for allegedly revealing "top secret military features" in court filings while insisting the facility is "vital to our National Security."

The administration's Friday filing cited the alleged "threat of a missile attack against Air Force One on July 8" to support its security argument, though some U.S. intelligence officials dispute the credibility of this Iranian threat claim.

Construction is "moving quickly towards completion," according to the administration, while the appeals court's two-week timeline gives the Supreme Court a narrow window to intervene before work resumes.
title: Trump accuses nonprofit organization of revealing ‘top military secrets’ in ballroom case

summary: Friday, the Justice Department issued a legal opinion granting U.S. military personnel broader powers to detain migrants accused of trespassing near designated National Defense Areas at the U.S.-Mexico border as part of President Trump's immigration crackdown.

President Trump's administration designated large swaths of land near the border as National Defense Areas, which the Defense Department controls to deter illegal immigration; these zones are closed to civilians and marked with warning signs in English and Spanish.

Deputy Assistant Attorney General William Hyde stated in Friday's opinion that using military personnel to arrest trespassers near an NDA does not violate the Posse Comitatus Act, citing "express statutory authorization and the military-purpose of a commander's traditional protective power."

Since the mission began, more than 20,000 service members have deployed to the border, where the administration has established six NDAs across Arizona, California, New Mexico, and Texas; this crackdown coincides with a significant decline in migrant apprehensions.

While the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel opinion is advisory, the military has suggested it may designate additional zones; U.S. Northern Command maintains that service members can apprehend trespassers and transfer them to appropriate law enforcement authorities.
title: Justice Department expands military's power to detain migrants accused of trespassing

summary: On Thursday, U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan warned the Justice Department he could hold attorneys in contempt over their handling of Jeffrey Epstein files , demanding compliance with court orders requiring justifications for redactions.

Journalist Katie Phang's lawsuit against Attorney General Todd Blanche alleges the government failed to comply with the Epstein Files Transparency Act, arguing it improperly redacted documents and withheld information referring to President Donald Trump.

Recalling his past handling of the Sen. Ted Stevens case, Sullivan warned he is willing to "enforce legitimate judicial orders." He pressed DOJ official Andrew Block for FBI notes, rejecting claims they were "substantially similar" to existing reports.
Attorney Brendan Ballou, representing Phang, denounced the department's "endless delay" and announced plans to file a proposed order regarding the Attorney General's noncompliance shortly.

Tensions persist as the department claims information will be "forthcoming," prompting Sullivan to quip, "Christmas is forthcoming," as the court remains focused on obtaining full transparency on redactions.
title: Judge’s Epstein Files Concerns Put Donald Trump's DOJ Under a New Spotlight

summary: Former Rep. Mary Peltola distanced herself from an endorsement by Vice President Kamala Harris on Friday as she seeks to flip a Senate seat in Republican-leaning Alaska.

Harris's Fight for the People PAC sent a fundraising email Wednesday urging donations to Peltola, declaring that if theres anyone who can flip Alaska and secure the Senate majority for Democrats its Mary.
A spokesperson told The New York Times the campaign neither approved nor knew about the email beforehand and said Peltola isnt seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48.
Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan's campaign immediately leveraged the endorsement to link Peltola to national Democrats, arguing the endorsement revealed which political team she represents.
Democrats need a net gain of four seats to overcome the 53-47 Senate majority held by Republicans, making Peltola one of the party's most important recruits.
title: Peltola distances herself from Kamala Harris endorsement ahead of Alaska primary

summary: On Friday, Amazon reinstated binding arbitration for its customers while barring them from seeking class-action lawsuits, making it more difficult for users to address grievances in court.

Five years ago, Amazon revoked binding arbitration after facing tens of thousands of costly individual cases. The company sought to address legal challenges that overwhelmed its administrative systems.
Amazon's new terms define 'mass arbitration' as 25 or more cases within a six-month period; such claims 'would be settled in' 'batches of at least 25.' This caps administrative burden.
A spokesperson said the clause will 'offer customers a fast, cost-effective way to resolve disputes' while still giving them the option of using small claims court.
Disputes with Amazon begun prior to Friday remain unaffected by the new terms. Customers agree to updated conditions by continuing to use the company's services.
title: Amazon reinstates binding arbitration, bars class-action lawsuits

summary: For the first time in 14 consecutive quarters, Berkshire Hathaway was a net buyer of equities, spending roughly $23.5 billion on purchases versus just $3.7 billion in sales during Q2.

Berkshire expanded its position in Alphabet by 83%, adding roughly 48 million shares to bring its total holding to nearly 106 million shares valued at ~$37.8 billion. This vaults the Google parent company into Berkshire's top three U.S.-listed stock holdings behind Apple and American Express.

A major portion of the Alphabet addition came via a $10 billion private placement completed in June—part of Alphabet's broader $80 billion capital raise to fund expanding artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Berkshire expanded its footprint in the housing sector by increasing its stake in Lennar by nearly 30% and initiating a new position in D.R. Horton. Shortly after the quarter ended, Berkshire also completed a $6.8 billion acquisition of homebuilder Taylor Morrison.

Berkshire significantly boosted its positions in Delta Air Lines and Macy's while completely exiting its stake in Constellation Brands and trimming existing holdings in Kroger, Bank of America, and Nucor.
title: Berkshire Hathaway boosted stake in Alphabet, homebuilders in the second quarter

summary: In Austin, Texas, the Democratic National Committee approved dueling policy positions on Saturday regarding ICE, reflecting internal party disagreement on how to oppose President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.
Following three fatal encounters in July, calls to abolish ICE intensified as a progressive rallying cry, renewing internal friction during the party's summer meeting.

DNC member Michele Johnson of Louisiana proposed the abolition measure, arguing the party must stop sounding "poll tested" and instead take a firm stance, citing the Naturalization Service as precedent.
Opposing the measure, Yvonne Reeves-Chong warned it would draw "fire" from voters and urged colleagues to prioritize winning races over symbolic positions.
Though the vote is not binding, broader dissatisfaction emerges; only 39% of U.S. adults approve of Trump's immigration performance, down from 49% earlier this year.
title: Democrats disagree over abolishing or reforming ICE at DNC meeting

Court records show Hickman was convicted in 2024 of misdemeanor fourth-degree child abuse and sentenced to one year in jail, with felony assault and sexual conduct charges dismissed.

Officers responded Friday morning to a home about 170 miles northwest of Detroit, where Michigan State Police found a 16-year-old boy, a 45-year-old man, and a 40-year-old woman dead; a 53-year-old man was later discovered at a second location.
Gov. Gretchen Whitmer said she is monitoring the situation and her thoughts are with the victims, while Ashley Miller of the MSP called the event heartbreaking for investigators.
A teenage girl survivor remains in stable condition while Miller said Saturday the investigation is ongoing; authorities are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the incident.

summary: Flooding along the White River in Indiana has killed at least five people, with emergency crews rescuing more than 90 individuals and their pets as record-breaking waters inundate neighborhoods across central Indiana.
More than 11 inches of rain fell over two days, pushing the White River past 24 feet in Anderson and Noblesville to surpass 1913 records. This record-breaking deluge triggered the historic flooding.

Indianapolis Fire Department spokesperson Rita Reith confirmed 91 people and 45 pets were rescued as of early afternoon Saturday. A 58-year-old woman in Delaware County died Friday after attempting to drive through floodwaters.
Governor Mike Braun declared a local emergency Friday and requested a federal declaration, which President Donald Trump intends to approve to support response and recovery efforts.

Forecasters warned additional showers and thunderstorms will move into central Indiana throughout Saturday, as Marion County Emergency Management Director Jacob Spence described the historic flooding as an 'unprecedented event.
title: Indiana authorities say at least 5 people have died in flooding across the state

summary: Since last fall, the Department of Homeland Security spent $464 million on 10 used aircraft it claimed were urgently needed for deportation flights, but the fleet has remained largely idle.

DHS bypassed competitive bidding by invoking an "unusual and compelling urgency" exemption for the contract, which went to Daedalus Aviation Corporation, led by William Walters, a doctor who donated $10,000 to a political committee connected to former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

Seven Boeing 737 passenger jets remain parked at an airport in Lake Charles, Louisiana, because the agency lacks personnel to operate them, while one luxury jet was leased to FBI Director Kash Patel for 12 months despite the FBI already having its own aircraft.

On Wednesday, Senate Democrats on the Appropriations Committee demanded a full accounting of the spending, stating "The American people deserve a full accounting of this gross misuse of their tax dollars." Officials told lawmakers four 737s might be repurposed for congressional travel.

Usage of the urgency exemption has surged from less than 1% of DHS spending in 2024 to nearly two-thirds of all contract dollars in 2026, covering projects from event planning to aircraft acquisitions.
title: DHS Bought $464 Million in Planes for Deportations, Then Left Most Idle: Report
topic_full: U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) · United States

summary: The Wall Street Journal reported that Stripe and private-equity firm Advent are negotiating to buy PayPal , with talks potentially concluding in the coming weeks.
Lores initiated a turnaround plan in April to address PayPal's recent struggles, splitting the business into three operating models and planning a 20% workforce reduction.
Stripe and Advent offered $60.50 a share in July, valuing PayPal at $53 billion, while Lores told investors PayPal would become a "technology company again."
PayPal declined to comment on the report, while a Stripe spokesperson said the company does not "comment on rumors or speculation" regarding the potential deal.
Founded in 1998 by Silicon Valley figures including Peter Thiel, Elon Musk, and Max Levchin, PayPal now faces a sale that could alter the strategic path Lores has been building since March.
title: Stripe and Advent bid $60.50 a share for PayPal as talks advance, WSJ reports

summary: Hurricane Lala strengthened into a Category 1 hurricane with 75 mph winds on Saturday, poised to strike the southern Big Island as the first direct hurricane threat in 155 years.

Tropical storm winds extend 220 miles from the center, threatening Oahu and Kauai by Sunday morning, while forecasters predict 8 to 12 inches of rain across lower elevations and up to 25 inches on Mauna Kea's higher slopes.

Officials warned residents in unpermitted structures to seek safe shelter as steep terrain faces life-threatening mudslides, while dry, breezy conditions outside the storm could trigger wildfires—a heightened concern following Lahaina's 2023 fire.

Emergency shelters opened and events were canceled as Gov. Josh Green described the system as "an enormous storm." Authorities urged ranchers to move cattle to pastures rather than structures that may collapse.

The Big Island has not experienced a direct hurricane landfall since 1871, when a Category 3 storm killed six people and destroyed thousands of homes. Warmer ocean temperatures and weakening upper-atmosphere winds are fueling increased Pacific hurricane activity this year.
title: Lala strengthens into a hurricane and bears down on Hawaii’s Big Island with heavy rain, winds

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the calendar as a “dramatically changed” nomination path, putting Black, Latino, and labor constituencies “front of the line,” while warning candidates face a “six-state gauntlet” that could help Democrats in 2028.

Right-Leaning coverage stresses that the party “abandons the traditional opening” in Iowa and New Hampshire, potentially leaving a “progressive presidential candidate at a disadvantage” and inviting legal challenges.
Center coverage is more procedural, detailing South Carolina on January 22, Nevada on February 1, and the six-state sequence.
All agree South Carolina leads, Iowa’s role changes, and diversity and electoral strategy drive the redesign.
summary: During its summer meeting in Austin, Texas, the Democratic National Committee officially approved a revised nominating calendar that establishes South Carolina as the first state to hold its 2028 presidential primary.

The approved schedule sets South Carolina's primary for January 22, 2028, followed in February by Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan, and Virginia as early-voting states before Super Tuesday.

Party leaders emphasized that prioritizing these specific early states ensures that Black, Latino, and union-member voters have an earlier and more influential voice in selecting the party's presidential nominee.
The new calendar completely excludes Iowa from the early-state lineup and removes its long-held position as the traditional opening contest of the Democratic nominating process.

Officials from displaced traditional early states, including Iowa and New Hampshire, strongly criticized the decision, arguing that it diminishes their historical role in vetting presidential candidates.
title: South Carolina to hold first 2028 Democratic presidential primary, DNC vote confirms

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Indiana’s flooding as a broad, “deadly” and “historic” crisis, emphasizing at least five deaths, more than 90 rescues, 170 voluntary evacuees, pets, and Noblesville’s emergency declaration.

The pivotal divide is scope and human cost, not policy: all perspectives stress severe storms, evacuations , rescues, official warnings, and an urgent public-safety threat.
summary: On Saturday, Noblesville Mayor Chris Jensen declared a state of emergency as the White River crested at approximately 24.6 feet, topping the 1913 record of 23.8 feet.
Severe storms caused widespread flash flooding across the region earlier this week, prompting Gov. Mike Braun to request a presidential emergency declaration to free up federal resources.

During a Saturday news conference, city officials reported that about 170 residents voluntarily evacuated affected areas, and the American Red Cross is providing assistance at the Hamilton County Fairgrounds.
Despite the historic flooding, the city's wastewater treatment plant remains operational, though officials noted Federal Hill Commons was designed to serve as a floodplain during high-water events.
By Saturday's news conference, the river had dropped to about 23.6 feet, though officials asked residents to conserve water as full recovery for Noblesville could take a couple of weeks.
title: Historic flooding prompts evacuations and water rescues in Indiana

summary: Police arrested Bronx resident Larry Montes, 46, on Friday after he disrupted Shabbat services at Central Synagogue in Manhattan and allegedly assaulted two individuals.
The incident occurred just after 6 p.m. at 642 Lexington Avenue, where authorities are investigating the disruption and assaults as potential hate crimes.
As synagogue security escorted him out, Montes allegedly struck a 63-year-old woman and spat at and headbutted a 65-year-old security guard, NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch confirmed.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani called the incident a "despicable act" with "no place in our city," while Tisch said the violation of her childhood synagogue was "deeply painful."
Additional NYPD resources have been deployed to Central Synagogue as a precaution, with authorities confirming there are no further threats to the community at this time.
title: Hate crime charges filed in Manhattan synagogue attack

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds Charlotte Touzalin’s distress and family’s “suffering,” “hope,” and the drugs’ “early promise,” while right-leaning coverage de-emphasizes biography and highlights a medical mechanism—possible improvement in insulin resistance alongside weight loss.
Center coverage occupies a middle ground, pairing “early” evidence with “puzzling symptoms” and patient impact.
Yet this is a modest framing difference, not a partisan clash: every version presents small, developing research, PMOS symptoms, and potential benefits beyond weight loss.
Even right-leaning wording retains “suffering family” and “hope,” underscoring shared human-interest emphasis rather than sharply opposed ideological narratives.
summary: Small but growing research shows GLP-1 obesity medications may treat polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome by promoting weight loss and improving insulin resistance, hormone balance and ovulation.
PMOS, renamed earlier this year to shift focus away from ovaries and cysts, affects 1 in 8 women worldwide; diagnosis often takes years because symptoms overlap with other conditions and vary widely.

Dr. Melanie Cree, who led three studies testing GLP-1 drugs for PMOS, said the results are 'incredibly effective and really exciting,' with participants losing a median of about 42 pounds and experiencing a 52% testosterone drop.

Charlotte Touzalin, an 18-year-old college student from Colorado, said she felt 'heard for the first time' after joining the study and became 'a happier version of myself,' though she stopped treatment in June when free access ended.

Dr. Rana Malek, an endocrinologist with the University of Maryland Medical System, cautioned that GLP-1s don't work for everyone and can cause side effects like nausea; she said it's 'frustrating that many can't get them because of insurance issues.
title: Small GLP-1 Studies Show Promise for PMOS Treatment

summary: On Friday, Dr. Anthony Fauci , former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases director, declined a request to voluntarily testify before a Senate subcommittee, with his attorneys arguing that compelling another appearance would "impermissibly harass or degrade Dr. Fauci for political purposes."

The refusal follows an August 6 vote by the Senate Homeland Security Committee to hold the former director in contempt, with the committee subsequently referring the matter to the Justice Department for potential investigation.

During a July 29 hearing, Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination 100 times while Republican Senators questioned him about pandemic policies and federal research funding, drawing sharp backlash from GOP members.

Sen. Ron Johnson, chairman of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, alleged Fauci "has a lot to hide" and announced the subcommittee will explore legal options to obtain records and speak with key individuals involved in the pandemic response.

Legal disputes persist over whether the presidential pardon invalidates Fauci's Fifth Amendment claims; Republican Sen. Rand Paul contends the pardon eliminates prosecution risk, while attorneys maintain it does not eliminate all legal threats, keeping Fauci central to ongoing investigations.
title: Dr. Anthony Fauci declines request to appear before a second Senate panel after GOP contempt vote
